newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worker compensation up 2.9 percent in 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worker compensation up 2.9 percent in 1996.

text.p: U.S. workers' compensation in the fourth quarter and all of 1996 rose slightly faster than the comparable periods a year earlier, the Labour Department said Tuesday.

Pay and benefits combined rose 2.9 percent last year, up from 2.7 percent in 1995, but smaller than the 3 percent gain of 1994, the department said. In the fourth quarter of last year, compensation rose 0.8 percent after a 0.6 percent gain in the third quarter.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had expected a slightly larger 0.9 percent rise in workers' compensation for the fourth quarter.

The U.S. Treasury bond rallied about a full percentage point immediately after the report was released, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year treasury bond falling to 6.85 percent from 6.94 percent late Monday.

"It shows the economy is moving ahead," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "Inflation is not getting out of hand and does not pose a threat of accelerating. That is the key."

Financial markets had been anxiously awaiting the Employment Cost Index data for indications of whether growing tightness in labour markets is raising salaries and benefit levels to the point where they could become an inflationary threat. Federal Reserve policymakers are also thought to be keeping close tabs on labour costs.
Quarterly compensation gains have ranged from 0.6 percent to 0.8 percent for the last three years, the department said.

The increase in compensation during the October-December period included a 0.8 percent rise in wages and salaries and a 0.7 percent rise in the cost of benefits, such as health care, received by employees, the department said. Both were up from increases of 0.6 percent in the third quarter of last year.
Wages and salaries, which represent about 70 percent of the index, rose 3.3 percent in the past 12 months -- the biggest gain since 1991 -- after a 2.9 percent rise in 1995.
Employers' costs for their workers' benefits rose 2 percent last year, down from 2.3 percent in 1995, the department said.

Benefit cost increases had been slowing late in 1995 and were flat in the first quarter of 1996 as employers shifted more of the burden of health care costs onto their workers. But in the last nine months of 1996, benefit costs increases have resumed growing at 0.6 to 0.7 percent each quarter.

Compensation gains for private industry workers in the fourth quarter rose 0.8 percent from 0.6 percent in the third quarter. For all of 1996, compensation rose 3.1 percent after rising 2.6 percent in 1995.

The 2.9 percent increase in the ECI for last year was more moderate than the 3.9 percent gain in workers' average hourly earnings over the same period, mostly because of the slower growth of benefit costs, which are not included in average hourly earnings.
